strengths: Clearly identifies and empirically demonstrates a real gap: existing training-free motion customization methods (e.g., MotionClone) fail when naively applied to distilled/few-step video generators, providing good motivating analysis (Fig. 2, Sec. 4.1).

The teacher-guided test-time distillation idea (endpoint prediction + interpolation between student and teacher one-step predictions) is a sensible and reasonably novel mechanism for injecting fine-grained motion guidance into a coarse-step model without retraining.

Comprehensive empirical validation: two backbone families (VideoCrafter2/T2V-Turbo-V2 and AnimateDiff/AnimateDiff-Lightning), multiple motion customization strategies (MotionClone, MotionDirector), multiple step budgets (16/8/4), and both training-based and training-free baselines.

Reasonably thorough ablation studies (Table 3, additional ablations on λ, η, k in supplementary) isolating the contribution of each component (motion guidance, inverted noise, teacher guidance, adaptive acceleration).
Includes a user study with a described protocol and reasonably large sample (50 participants, 36 pairs), which strengthens the claim of qualitative superiority beyond automated metrics.
Extensive qualitative supplementary results covering diverse motion types (object, camera, hybrid) support generalization claims.

The adaptive acceleration strategy (step-wise activation + dynamic truncation) is a practical contribution that meaningfully reduces inference cost relative to naive teacher guidance at every step (20s -> 13s in ablation) while retaining most quality gains.
weaknesses: The method is not fully "training-free" in a resource-light sense: it requires loading and running a full high-quality teacher model at test time in addition to the student, which is a substantial practical overhead not deeply discussed as a limitation (only briefly mentioned in future work about quality-checking, not about the dual-model memory/compute burden).

Novelty is somewhat incremental: it largely recombines existing components (MotionClone's motion loss/energy function, DMT/MotionDirector-style noise blending, and generic teacher-student score distillation) rather than introducing a fundamentally new algorithmic idea; the main new pieces are the interpolation-based teacher-student coupling and the adaptive scheduling heuristics.

Key hyperparameters (δ1, δ2, k, λ, η) appear to be manually tuned per motion type/model (e.g., δ1 ranging 380-420 "according to motion types"), raising concerns about generalizability and the practical burden of tuning for new domains/models without clear guidance on how to set them automatically.

Quantitative metrics used (CLIP-based temporal consistency and text alignment, FID against a self-constructed reference set) have known limitations (e.g., temporal consistency can reward blurriness) and the FID reference-set construction process is not clearly specified, making some quantitative claims harder to fully trust.
No variance/error bars or multiple-seed results are reported for the quantitative comparisons, so the statistical robustness of the reported improvements is unclear.

Benchmark scale is modest (66 video-edit pairs from 22 videos for TurboBench, 15 videos for AnimateBench), which may limit the strength of generalization claims despite broad qualitative diversity shown in supplementary.

The efficiency comparison, while favorable relative to many baselines, still shows the full method (13s/24s) is notably slower than the naive motion-guidance-on-distilled-model baseline (6-9s), so the described "high efficiency" claim is relative rather than absolute; this trade-off could be more explicitly contextualized in the main text.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem diagnosis: the paper convincingly shows (Fig. 2, Table 3) that existing training-free motion customization methods (MotionClone, DiTFlow) fail on distilled few-step video generators because coarse denoising steps and altered generative dynamics are incompatible with dense-trajectory score guidance.

The proposed teacher-guided test-time distillation mechanism is technically sound: the SDS-style decomposition that avoids backpropagating through the student network Jacobian is clearly derived, with a closed-form linear interpolation update, and the appendix provides a rigorous derivation (clean-space update, equivalent proximal form, and noise-prediction form), aiding reproducibility.

The adaptive acceleration strategy (step-wise guidance activation + dynamic truncation) is a sensible and well-ablated efficiency mechanism (Tables 3-5) that meaningfully reduces inference time while retaining most of the quality gains from teacher guidance.

Extensive and diverse experimental validation: the method is tested across many distilled backbones (T2V-Turbo-V2, Video-Blade, AnimateDiff-Lightning, Wan2.1/2.2 variants, CogVideoX-2B/TDM) and multiple motion-guidance objectives (MotionClone, MOFT, DMT, DiTFlow), on two main benchmarks plus an additional LOVEU-TGVE benchmark, with quantitative metrics, qualitative comparisons, a user study, and compute/memory analysis, altogether making the empirical case for generality and efficiency fairly convincing.

Consistent efficiency-quality trade-off improvement over baselines: MotionEcho achieves substantially lower inference time than both training-free (up to ~35x) and training-based (up to ~400x) alternatives while improving or matching motion fidelity and other quality metrics.
Honest discussion of limitations (failure case with fine-grained motion misalignment, Fig. 8) and a substantive ethical/social impact discussion that goes beyond boilerplate.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution is largely a careful engineering combination of existing ideas (score distillation sampling-style decoupled optimization, existing training-free motion guidance losses such as MotionClone/DiTFlow, and adaptive scheduling), rather than a fundamentally new algorithmic principle; novelty lies mainly in the integration and adaptation to the distillation setting.

The method requires loading and repeatedly querying a full-size teacher diffusion model at inference time, which increases peak GPU memory substantially (up to 36GB for TurboV2 backbone per Table 12) and reintroduces a dependency on the very full-diffusion models the distilled generator was meant to replace; this tension with the "efficiency of distilled generation" framing could be discussed more directly in the main text.

Quantitative gains over baselines are sometimes marginal or mixed on certain metrics (e.g., in Table 1 MotionClone already attains TC=0.978, slightly above MotionEcho's 0.976/0.967/0.956 variants), and no variance/error bars are reported across runs or seeds, making it hard to assess the statistical robustness of the reported improvements.

Applicability presumes availability of a compatible high-quality teacher model with shared or bridgeable latent space; the paper itself notes in future work that unpaired teacher models with unshared latent spaces remain unsolved, which limits generality to settings where a well-matched teacher is unavailable (e.g., some closed-source or heavily customized distilled models).

The main text is notation-dense and compresses many method details (motion loss, adaptive scheduling criteria) that are only fully clarified in the appendix; a reader relying solely on the main paper may find the mechanism harder to follow without cross-referencing supplementary material.

Motion fidelity and other metrics rely on learned trackers/CLIP embeddings (Co-Tracker, CLIP), which are known to have their own biases and may not fully capture perceptual motion fidelity; while a Flow-sim metric is added in the appendix as a partial mitigation, this is not the primary reported metric in the main tables.

strengths: Identifies and clearly diagnoses a real, practically important problem: existing training-free motion-customization techniques (designed for full multi-step diffusion models) break down when applied directly to fast distilled video generators, due to coarse large denoising steps and altered trajectory dynamics. The diagnostic experiments (Fig. 2, Sec. 3.2) convincingly motivate the method.

The proposed teacher-guided test-time distillation (score interpolation / 'echo') is technically grounded: the paper derives the closed-form clean-space interpolation update, shows its equivalence to a proximal problem and to a noise-prediction-space correction, providing a principled justification rather than an ad hoc heuristic.

Extensive empirical validation across a wide variety of distilled backbones (UNet-based TurboV2, DiT-based Video-Blade/Wan2.1-1.3B, AnimateDiff-Lightning, Wan2.2-T2V-5B variants, CogVideoX-2B/TDM) and multiple motion-representation methods (MotionClone, MOFT, DMT, DiTFlow), demonstrating good architecture-agnostic generality.

Comprehensive quantitative evaluation on two/three benchmarks (TurboBench, DavisBench, plus LOVEU-TGVE in the appendix), thorough ablations isolating the contribution of motion guidance, teacher guidance, and adaptive acceleration (Table 3, Fig. 7), and hyperparameter sensitivity studies (Tables 4-5).

Efficiency-quality trade-off is explicitly quantified (inference time, GPU memory, FID/MF/TC/TA), and the adaptive acceleration mechanism is shown to substantially cut inference cost while retaining most of the quality gains.
User study with 50 participants corroborates the quantitative motion-fidelity and visual-quality claims.

Honest limitations discussion with a concrete failure case (fine-grained motion mismatch across dissimilar subjects, Fig. 8) and a considered ethical/social impact discussion; reasonable reproducibility support via pseudocode (Algorithm 1) and detailed hyperparameter/implementation appendix.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution—applying SDS-style teacher correction with re-noise/interpolate to bridge student and teacher trajectories—is a reasonably natural combination of existing ideas (motion energy guidance from MotionClone/DiTFlow/DMT/MOFT + score distillation sampling concepts), so the degree of algorithmic novelty is moderate rather than groundbreaking.

The method still requires running a full (non-distilled) teacher diffusion model at inference time; although the adaptive scheduling mitigates its cost, this dependency reduces the 'pure' efficiency advantage of distilled generators and may not be applicable when a compatible paired teacher (shared latent/architecture) is unavailable — the paper itself flags unpaired teachers as unresolved future work.

Some reported metrics show the method does not uniformly dominate baselines (e.g., Table 1: MotionClone's TC of 0.978 is marginally higher than Ours-16steps at 0.976), and it is not always fully transparent whether reported inference-time-cost figures for the method include the teacher's compute overhead in a directly comparable way across tables.

The framework relies on a fairly large number of hyperparameters (τ, λ, η, k, δ1, δ2, W, N_max) that are stated to be 'fixed... without careful tuning' across experiments; while ablations on one backbone (TurboV2) show some robustness, generalization of these fixed settings to new motion types/backbones is not deeply verified.

Benchmarks (TurboBench, DavisBench, AnimateBench) are custom constructions from existing video sources, and details such as per-class sample sizes for the FID reference sets are not fully specified, which could affect the reliability/reproducibility of FID comparisons.

Qualitative comparisons are selectively curated to highlight favorable cases for the proposed method; broader failure-mode analysis beyond the single discussed case (object identity mismatch) would strengthen the honesty of the evaluation.
